questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equation of an Osculating Plane
questions.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,T(0)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The vectors $T(0)$ and $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩=⟨0,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(0,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+s\,T(0)+u\,N(0) \\  & =⟨0,1,1⟩+s\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}⟨-1,-1,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3},\,1-\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2},\,1+\frac{s\sqrt{3}}{3}-\frac{u\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Recomputing gives r(0)=⟨0,1,1⟩, r′(0)=⟨1,-1,1⟩ and r″(0)=⟨0,-1,-1⟩. Thus the actual osculating plane is 2x+y-z=0. The supplied T(0)=⟨-1,-1,1⟩/√3 contradicts r′(0)/‖r′(0)‖. Using that supplied tangent in r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0) produces option e, but its plane is -2x+y-z=0. Options a, b, c and d describe x+z=-1, x=√3, x=√3 and x+y-z=2, respectively. None is the actual osculating plane. The earlier uncertainty therefore remains justified by the contradictory tangent data.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equation of an Osculating Plane
questions.problem:
Find the equation of the osculating plane (in parametric form) for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(-1,0,1)$ where $t=\pi $, given that

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\pi )=\frac{3}{5}\,i-\frac{4}{5}k,\,N(\pi )=-j.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(-1,0,1)$ is $r(\pi )=-i+\,k.$

The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector $r(1).$ The vectors $T(1)$ and $N(1)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, the equation of the plane (in parametric form) can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

Hence, the equation of the osculating plane at the point $(-1,0,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ) \\  & =(-i+\,k)+s(\frac{3}{5}\,i-\frac{4}{5}k)+u(-\,j) \\  & =(-1+\frac{3}{5}s)\,i-u\,j+(1-\frac{4}{5}s)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\pi ,$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,T(\pi )=\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩,\,N(\pi )=⟨-1,0,0⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(\pi ).$ The vectors $T(\pi )$ and $N(\pi )$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\pi ) & =⟨-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi ,\,4\pi ,3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi ⟩=⟨3,4\pi ,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(3,4\pi ,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(\pi )+s\,T(\pi )+u\,N(\pi ) \\  & =⟨3,4\pi ,0⟩+s\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩+u⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =⟨3-u,\,4\pi +\frac{4s}{5},\,-\frac{3s}{5}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
r(t)=⟨{e}^{t},\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,T(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩
$$

where $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point that is at the tip of the vector $r(0).$ The unit tangent vector $T(0)$ and the principal normal vector $N(0)$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as 

$$
R(s,u)=r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0),\,s,\,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(0) & =⟨{e}^{0},\,{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(1,\,0,\,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(0)+sT(0)+uN(0) \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩+s\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,1,\,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}},\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}},\,1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{3}}-\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
r(t)=⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩,\,T(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,0,1⟩,\,N(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,-1,0⟩.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P$, which is at the tip of the vector $r(\frac{\pi }{2}).$ The vectors $T((\frac{\pi }{2})$ and $N(\frac{\pi }{2})$ are parallel to this plane. Therefore, a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
R(s,u)=r(\frac{\pi }{2})+s\,T(\frac{\pi }{2})+u\,N(\frac{\pi }{2}),\,s,u\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

 

We have that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨2,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})⟩=⟨2,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $(2,1,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(\frac{\pi }{2})+s\,T(\frac{\pi }{2})+u\,N(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =⟨2,1,0⟩+s⟨0,0,1⟩+u⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,1-u,\,s⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of an Osculating Plane
questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0$, given that

$$
r(t)=⟨-2t,\,{t}^{2},\,-{t}^{2}⟩,\,T(0)=⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩,\,N(0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩
$$

where $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
The position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}p=r(0) & =⟨-2(0),\,{0}^{2},\,{0}^{2}⟩=⟨0,\,0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =⟨-1,\,0,\,0⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,\,-1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=-\sqrt{2}\cdot (T(0)\times N(0))=⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩ & =⟨0,0,0⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,1,\,1⟩ \\ 0\cdot x+1\cdot y+1\cdot z & =0 \\ y+z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of an Osculating Plane
questions.problem:
Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1,3)$ where $t=0,$ given that

$$
T(0)=i,\,N(0)=j.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(0,1,3)$ is $p=⟨0,1,3⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =i\times j \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(0)\times N(0)=k=⟨0,0,1⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩ & =⟨0,1,3⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩ \\ x(0)+y(0)+z(1) & =0(0)+1(0)+3(1) \\ 0+0+z & =0+0+3 \\ z-3 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for a curve $r(t)$ at the point $P(0,1,2)$ where $t=\pi ,$ given that

$$
T(\pi )=i,\,N(\pi )=-k.
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the position vector of the point $P(0,1,2)$ is $p=⟨0,1,2⟩.$

To find the equation of the osculating plane, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to it. To do that, we find the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1)\times N(1) & =i\times (-k) \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(\pi )\times N(\pi )=j=⟨0,1,0⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a general point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ & =⟨0,1,2⟩\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\ x(0)+y(1)+z(0) & =0(0)+1(1)+2(0) \\ 0+y+0 & =0+1+0 \\ y-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2,\,-{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=0$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡0+\operatorname{cos}⁡0,\,0,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡0-\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\ N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,0,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡0+\operatorname{sin}⁡0⟩=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
p=r(0)=⟨{e}^{0}\operatorname{sin}⁡0,\,2,\,-{e}^{0}\operatorname{cos}⁡0⟩=⟨0,2,-1⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(0)$ and the principal normal $N(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\times N(0) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,-1⟩\times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨1,0,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨0,-2,0⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our perpendicular vector $n$ is 

$$
n=T(0)\times N(0)=⟨0,-1,0⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ & =⟨0,2,-1⟩\cdot ⟨0,-1,0⟩ \\ x(0)+y(-1)+z(0) & =0(0)+2(-1)+(-1)(0) \\ 0-y+0 & =0-2+0 \\ y-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\ T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},3\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},4\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨0,3,4⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-1,0,0⟩\times (-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,4⟩) \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ -1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 4\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}⟨0,4,-3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the above vector, let's write our perpendicular vector $n$ as 

$$
n=(-5)\cdot (T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}))=⟨0,4,-3⟩.
$$

Finally, let $⟨x,y,z⟩$ denote the position vector of a point on the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $n$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $p$, its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ & =⟨0,3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,-3⟩ \\ 0\cdot x+4\cdot y+(-3)\cdot z & =0 \\ 4y-3z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Shortest Distance Between an Osculating Plane and the Origin
questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=1,$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =6t\,i+2{t}^{3}\,j+3\sqrt{2}{t}^{2}\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}(i+{t}^{2}\,j+\sqrt{2}tk) \\ N(t) & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}(-\sqrt{2}t\,i+\sqrt{2}t\,j+(1-{t}^{2})k)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=1$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(i+1\,j+\sqrt{2}k)=\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k) \\ N(1) & =\frac{1}{1+1}(-\sqrt{2}\,i+\sqrt{2}\,j+(1-1)k)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point  where $t=1$ is

$$
p=r(1)=6\,i+2\,j+3\sqrt{2}\,k.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(1)$ and the principal normal $N(1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(1)\times N(1) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j+\sqrt{2}k)k\times (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j)) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}⟨-\sqrt{2},-\sqrt{2},2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨6,2,3\sqrt{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{2}⟨-1,-1,\sqrt{2}⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{2}|-6-2+6| \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Shortest Distance Between an Osculating Plane and the Origin
questions.problem:
Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $r(t)$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-1⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $T$ and $N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that the unit tangent and the principal normal at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-1⟩=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},-\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},0⟩=⟨-1,0,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the position vector of the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}$ is

$$
p=r(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨2\operatorname{sin}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,2\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{2},\,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩=⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩.
$$

Now, we need to find a vector that's perpendicular to the osculating plane. To do that, we use the cross product of the unit tangent $T(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and the principal normal $N(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\times N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,-1,-1⟩\times ⟨-1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(j-k) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
d=\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖}=|p\cdot n|,
$$

since $‖n‖=1.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|p\cdot n| \\  & =|⟨2,0,-\frac{\pi }{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨0,1,-1⟩| \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|0+0+\frac{\pi }{2}| \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\pi \sqrt{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

mathematical_assessment.explanation: Independent rechecking confirms the contradiction. The curve gives r′(π/2)=⟨0,-2,-1⟩ and r″(π/2)=⟨-2,0,0⟩, whose cross product is ⟨0,2,-4⟩. Through r(π/2)=⟨2,0,-π/2⟩, the actual osculating plane is y-2z=π, with distance π/√5. No displayed choice equals this. The supplied T instead gives normal ⟨0,1,-1⟩/√2 and distance π√2/4 (d), but T is not tangent to the stated curve. This inconsistency explains the earlier uncertainty.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Parametric Equation of an Osculating Plane
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14083925/assets/1990d7cb1625ca97f10debf834883f6e434473f154cf9683db60ee7c4a69c83e.png)

Find a parametric equation of the osculating plane for the curve  $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=1,$ given that

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \left\langle -2t , \: t^2 , \: \dfrac{1}{3}t^3 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf T(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle -2 , 2 , 1 \right\rangle, \qquad
\mathbf N(1) = \dfrac{1}{3}\left\langle 2 , 1 , 2\right\rangle.
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The osculating plane passes through the point $P,$ which is at the tip of the vector $\mathbf r(1).$ The vectors $\mathbf T(1)$ and $\mathbf N(1)$ are parallel to this plane and are not collinear, so a parametric equation for the plane can be written as

$$
\mathbf R(s,u) = \mathbf r(1) + s \, \mathbf T(1) + u \, \mathbf N(1), \qquad s,u \in (-\infty, \infty).
$$

 

Computing $\mathbf r(1),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(1) & =⟨-2(1),\,(1)^{2},\,\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}⟩=⟨-2,1,\frac{1}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a parametric equation for the osculating plane at the point $\left(-2,1,\dfrac 1 3 \right)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s,u) & =r(1)+s\,T(1)+u\,N(1) \\  & =⟨-2,1,\frac{1}{3}⟩+s\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,2,1⟩+u\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-6-2s+2u,\,3+2s+u,\,1+s+2u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Equation of an Osculating Plane
canonical_examples.problem:
Find a Cartesian equation of the osculating plane for the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=0,$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ T(t) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\ N(t) & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡tk).\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=0$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(0) = \cos{0}\,\mathbf i+\cos{0}\,\mathbf j+\sqrt{2}\sin{0}\, \mathbf k = \langle 1, 1, 0 \rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we first need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T(0)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N(0)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,k)=k \\ N(0) & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡0\,j+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡0k)=-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =k\times (-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)) \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(-i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 2}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\left(\mathbf i-\mathbf j\right) =\mathbf i-\mathbf j
$$

Finally, let $\langle x,y,z \rangle$ denote the position vector of a general point in the osculating plane. Since the plane is perpendicular to $\mathbf{n}$ and passes through the tip of the position vector $\mathbf{p},$ its Cartesian equation can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}(⟨x,y,z⟩-p)\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n-p\cdot n & =0 \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot n & =p\cdot n \\ ⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ & =⟨1,1,0⟩\cdot ⟨1,-1,0⟩ \\ 1\cdot x+(-1)\cdot y+0\cdot z & =0 \\ x-y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14083925/assets/ad22c676123844c2428febb34e0218cfcb05917154e8cff994f35fa4fbf68944.png)

**Note:** Because our curve is a plane curve, it has the same osculating plane at each point. As shown above, the osculating plane coincides with the plane of the curve. 

This result holds in general: any plane curve has the same osculating plane at each of its points (wherever the osculating plane is defined).

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Shortest Distance Between an Osculating Plane and the Origin
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14083925/assets/46e9f26846b088dfe225b36b889c788ed847c08376295f02dc2c9fbaf72a1645.png)

Find the shortest distance between the origin and the osculating plane for the curve $\mathbf r(t)$ at the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ given that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,8t⟩ \\ T(t) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,4⟩ \\ N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡6t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡6t,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\mathbf T$ and $\mathbf N$ denote the unit tangent and principal normal, respectively.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To calculate the Cartesian equation of the osculating plane, we need to compute the position vector $\mathbf p$ and a vector $\mathbf n$ that is perpendicular to the osculating plane. 

The position vector of the point where $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ is

$$
\mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \left\langle \sin{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)} , \:  -\cos{\left(6\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)}, \: 8\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \right\rangle  = \left\langle -1, 0, 2\pi \right\rangle.
$$

To compute the perpendicular vector, we need to compute the unit tangent $\mathbf T \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right)$ and the principal normal $\mathbf N \left( \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,4⟩=\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩ \\ N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}),\,0⟩=⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take the cross product of these two vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =T(\frac{\pi }{4})\times N(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,-3,4⟩\times ⟨1,0,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\cdot \left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & -3 & 4 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\text{ }\left|\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,i-\left|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,j+\left|\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k\text{ }] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\,j+3\,k) \\  & =⟨0,\frac{4}{5},\frac{3}{5}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Since we are interested only in the direction of the vector above, we can multiply it by a constant to yield a simpler vector that points in the same direction:

$$
\mathbf{n} = 5\cdot \left\langle 0 , \dfrac{4}{5} , \dfrac{3}{5} \right\rangle = \langle 0, 4, 3  \rangle
$$

Finally, the shortest distance between our plane and the origin is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\frac{|(p-0)\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|p\cdot n|}{‖n‖} \\  & =\frac{|⟨-1,0,2\pi ⟩\cdot ⟨0,4,3⟩|}{‖⟨0,4,3⟩‖} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
